item.text: {"text":"Recent evidence supports separating gradient direction, magnitude and sampling effects. [DARE (ICLR 2025)](https://ise.thss.tsinghua.edu.cn/~mlong/doc/Long-Sequence-Recommendation-ICLR25.pdf) finds conflicting attention/representation embedding gradients in roughly two-thirds of cases, with representation gradients about five times larger; this concerns attention-based CTR models, so transfer to NextItNet remains a hypothesis. [Negative-sampling experiments (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) show aggregate accuracy can conceal head/mid/tail disparities and sampler-dependent popularity bias. [gBCE (2024)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939) identifies overconfidence and unstable BCE training under negative sampling, motivating loss diagnostics without replacing the NextItNet backbone.\n\nProposed adaptation: compute per-example gradients separately for each dilated residual block and item embeddings; report gradient norms, pairwise cosine conflict rates and alignment with validation-loss gradients. Stratify by training-item frequency and recent-history coherence measured from available histories or titles. Separate positive/negative loss contributions, fix sampled negatives when comparing probes, and exclude padding. These are diagnostic proposals, not established NextItNet findings. [Final-model-only attribution (NeurIPS 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03906) treats gradient attribution as an approximation to sensitivity under further training; first-order accuracy can deteriorate as updates accumulate. Test predicted effects using small, norm-bounded updates restricted to an implicated block or embedding rows, restoring the same checkpoint after every intervention and comparing with matched random controls. Measure actual validation loss, ranking margins and pinned macro HR@10: reduced conflict or large gradients alone establish neither a failure mechanism nor recommendation gains. Retain one trained NextItNet checkpoint per category."}
